title: The Ticket Machine That Kept the Coins

post.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
post.title: I finish my late great-aunt's machines at night. The ticket machine I finished for a cliff railway kept £46 from 23 riders in Thursday's rush and printed them nothing. Its own log saw every coin.

blocks.text: My great-aunt Winifrith Torvaine built coin machines and clockwork figures for sixty years, and wrote small programs for local firms in her last ten. She died in the spring and left me her workshop of unfinished machines, each with a paper work order tied on with string. I program on night shifts, and I finish her machines at night.

This order came from the Sornmouth Cliff Railway: two cars on rails up the cliff from the harbour, one rising while the other comes down. A ride costs £2, and the bottom station's ticket machine takes £2 coins only. Inside, a coin drops into a holding cup. Then one of two things happens: the cup tips into the cash box when a ticket starts printing, or it opens into the return tray, which hands the coin back.

Winifrith's program remembers three flags. A flag is a yes-or-no value, like a light switch that is on or off: hasCoin, printing and noPaper. Beside them she wrote: *Three lamps can show eight pictures. A good machine only ever shows four.*

Anything that happens to the machine is called an event: a coin drops, someone presses the ticket button or the cancel button, or the printer finishes, which I call printed. For each event, the program first checks the flags, then acts, then sets new flags. Each block below is one event:

coin:    if noPaper: cup to tray, stop
         hasCoin = yes
button:  if hasCoin and not printing:
           cup to box; printing = yes
printed: printing = no; hasCoin = no
         if roll empty: noPaper = yes
cancel:  if hasCoin and not printing:
           cup to tray; hasCoin = no

A ticket takes 4 seconds (s) to print. It went in on Monday 7 September, and the box matched the ticket counter every evening. On Thursday at noon the railway opened a contactless gate beside the machine: riders tap a bank card and walk straight through. That evening the coin queue hurried to keep up.

Aneira, the bottom-station attendant, puts an empty cash box in at 17:30 and takes it out at 18:30. Thursday's held £128. The counter said 41 tickets, which is £82. Her tally sheet had 23 marks for "it ate my £2". She wrote each of those riders a paper pass so they could ride.
The machine logs every event: the time, the event, then hasCoin, printing and noPaper after it. Here are two riders at 17:41:

17:41:20  coin     yes  no   no
17:41:21  button   yes  yes  no
17:41:23  coin     yes  yes  no
17:41:24  button   yes  yes  no
17:41:25  printed  no   no   no
17:41:29  button   no   no   no
17:41:35  cancel   no   no   no

The first rider took a ticket at 17:41:25. The second dropped a coin at 17:41:23, while that ticket printed. Their button, and later their cancel, did nothing. At 17:41:36 they gave up and went to Aneira. Their £2 sat in the cup until the next rider's ticket tipped it into the box.
The machine never lost a coin. It forgot one.

Aneira emailed me the count at 18:40. Nobody's money is missing: the 23 coins are in the box, and her passes stood in for the tickets. But 23 riders believe a machine robbed them. What should I change before the first car at 07:00?

blocks.label: ticket_log_1741_redrawn.png

diagram.aria: Twenty seconds from 17:41:18. The printer runs from 17:41:21 to 17:41:25. hasCoin is yes from 17:41:20 to 17:41:25, then no. The first rider's coin is in the cup from 17:41:20 to 17:41:21. The second rider's coin is in the cup from 17:41:23 to the end. The second rider waits from 17:41:23 until giving up at 17:41:36.

blocks.caption: I redrew the log as a timeline, 20 seconds from 17:41:18. The first rider's coin sits in the cup for a second until the button tips it into the box at 17:41:21, and the printer runs until 17:41:25. The second rider's coin drops at 17:41:23, while hasCoin is already yes. At 17:41:25 printed sets hasCoin to no, but the coin stays in the cup. The second rider presses the button at 17:41:29 and cancel at 17:41:35, and gives up at 17:41:36.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: You met the word state in the lift case (w03): which one of a fixed set of situations a machine is in right now, like a traffic light showing one colour. Count first. Three flags, each yes or no, give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations. List all eight, and beside each write the situation it stands for, if any. Then read your 17:41:23 line. Before that coin, hasCoin was already yes. Whose coin was that yes about, and where was that coin by then? And at 17:41:25, which coin did hasCoin = no forget?

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: Four of the eight are real states: waiting (no, no, no), has money (yes, no, no), printing (yes, yes, no) and no paper (no, no, yes). The other four can't happen, and nothing says what they would do. The yes during printing was about the first rider's coin, which went into the box at 17:41:21.

comments.author: u/hands_off_while_busy_gesine
comments.text: Printing is the one moment a machine must not be disturbed. Good machines lock out input while they work: a lift ignores its buttons while the doors move, a till ignores keys mid-receipt. Ignore every coin while printing is yes, and the only bad moment in your machine is gone. One line, nothing else to break.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: The slot has no shutter. Whatever the program does, a coin that goes in drops into the cup.

comments.author: u/one_more_flag_blazena
comments.text: Your bug is one missing flag. Add coinNext: a coin that drops while printing sets it, and printed copies it into hasCoin. Four lines. Someone will tell you to make each state an object (s5e04: a bundle of values plus its methods, the actions it can do). For a ticket machine that's a cathedral built to hold one coin.

replies.author: u/workshop_nights_odgerel
replies.text: The railway's engineer suggested a middle way: one value holding the state's name, and in each event's code a switch. A switch is a list of cases, one per state name, each with its own lines; the program runs the case that matches.

reply.prompt: The first car runs at 07:00, and the evening rush comes again tomorrow. What should Odgerel change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Ignore any coin that drops while printing is yes, so nothing can disturb a print.
options.part2: I added one line: while printing is yes, a coin event does nothing. Before it went in, I replayed Thursday's rush from the log on Winifrith's workbench. It came out the same to the coin: 41 tickets, 23 riders with nothing, £46 in the box with no ticket. At 17:41:23 the second rider's coin still dropped into the cup, because the slot has no shutter, and at 17:41:25 printed still set hasCoin to no. Before, the program miscounted that coin; now it refused even to hear it. I didn't send it. Until a real fix went in, Aneira taped a card over the slot: wait for your ticket before you pay. She still had to watch every coin rider, and on Friday's rush she wrote passes again.
options.senior: Ignoring input is only safe when the input can be refused. Here it can't: the coin is already in the cup whatever the program decides, so ignoring it just means losing track of real money. The fault was never that printing was disturbed; it was that the flags had no way to say 'printing, and a new coin is waiting'. Locking out an event only moves the blank square; it doesn't answer it.

options.text: Keep one state name, and give each event a switch with a case for every state.
options.part2: I replaced the three flags with one value holding the state's name: waiting, has money, printing or no paper. Each of the four events became a switch with four cases. In printing, a coin goes straight to the tray and the lamp says wait for the ticket. On the workbench, Thursday's rush gave 64 tickets for 64 coins, and nobody left with nothing. The second 17:41 rider got the coin back at 17:41:23, put it in again at 17:41:26 and had a ticket at 17:41:31. With the roll down to its last 14 tickets, the machine went to no paper at 17:41:25 and handed that rider's coin back again at 17:41:26. It went in on Friday morning, and Friday's box matched the counter. Then the railway asked for a jammed state, for when the printer jams. That meant a new case in all four switches, and on the bench I caught that I had added it to three.
options.senior: A state name with a switch per event is honest: the machine is always in one named state, so the meaningless combinations are gone and every square can be written. It is correct here. The cost is where the rules live: one state's behaviour is split across every event's switch, so each new state is an edit to all of them, and a missed case quietly does nothing, which is Thursday's bug in a new place. Fine for a machine that will never grow; for one that will, keep each state's rules together.

options.text: Add a fourth flag, coinNext, for a coin that drops in while printing is yes.
options.part2: I added coinNext: a coin that drops while printing sets it, and printed copies it into hasCoin. On the workbench, Thursday's rush came out right: 64 tickets, and the second 17:41 rider's press at 17:41:29 had their ticket out at 17:41:33. It went in on Friday morning. Then I replayed the rush with the roll down to its last 14 tickets. The first 17:41 rider took ticket 14 at 17:41:25, and printed set hasCoin and noPaper both to yes, a picture Winifrith's program had never been able to show. The button doesn't check noPaper, because it never had to. At 17:41:29 it tipped the second rider's £2 into the box and ran the printer for 4 s with no paper; their cancel at 17:41:35 did nothing. One rider with nothing, £2 kept. Until I could change it, I asked Aneira to put a fresh roll in before every rush.
options.senior: Each flag doubles the combinations: three flags make 8, four make 16, and every one the code doesn't name is a place where the machine does something nobody chose. coinNext fixed the one combination Thursday found and created a new one, coin held with no paper, that the button was never written for. Patching flags turns every fix into a search for the next impossible picture. Name the states instead, so the machine can only ever be in one of them.

options.text: Make each of the four states an object that decides what every event does.
options.part2: I gave the machine one object per state: waiting, has money, printing and no paper. Each has the same four methods, one per event, and the machine hands every event to the object for its current state. Printing's coin method opens the cup into the tray and lights 'wait for the ticket'; its printed method moves the machine to waiting, or to no paper if the roll is empty. Every method is written, even as 'can't happen: log it'. On the workbench, Thursday's rush gave 64 tickets for 64 coins. The second 17:41 rider got the coin back at 17:41:23, put it in again at 17:41:26 and had a ticket at 17:41:31. With the roll down to its last 14 tickets, the state went to no paper at 17:41:25 and the coin came back again at 17:41:26: nobody lost a coin. It went in on Friday morning, and Friday's box matched the counter. When the railway asked for a jammed state, I wrote one new class and changed one method, printing's printed.
options.senior: This is the state pattern: each state is an object that answers every event, and the machine passes each event to whichever object is current. There are no flags to combine, so a meaningless picture can't exist; one state's rules sit together, so a blank shows up in one place; and a new state is a new class rather than an edit to every event. The cost runs the other way: a new event, such as a return-ticket button, needs a method in every state class. Choose it when states grow faster than events, as they usually do in machines like this.

sim.title: Replay the rush on Winifrith's workbench
sim.lede: You're Odgerel at the workbench, replaying Thursday 15 October's coin riders from 17:29:50, before the rush. 41 groups step up 85 s apart from 17:30:00; 23 of them are pairs, whose second rider steps up 3 s after the first, 2 s into the first rider's 4 s print. Each rider puts in a £2 coin and presses the button 1 s later if the coin was kept. A rider with nothing after 6 s presses the button again, after 12 s presses cancel, and after 13 s gives up and tells Aneira. A rider whose coin is handed back while another ticket prints puts it in again 1 s after the printer stops. Pick a design: as built with three flags; coins ignored while printing; a fourth flag, coinNext; one state name with a switch in each event; or one object per state. Pick the roll: 300 tickets left at 17:30, or 14. The table shows what the design does in each situation for each event.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press step nine times and read the 17:41:23 and 17:41:25 lines. Play the rest: 23 riders with nothing and £46 with no ticket. Try ignoring coins: the same. Try the fourth flag: right, until you set the roll to 14 tickets and watch rider 15 at 17:41:29. Then try one object per state on both rolls, and compare its methods to change for a jammed state with the switch's.

explain.oneLine: No coin was lost and nothing broke. hasCoin was already yes while a ticket printed, so a second rider's coin changed nothing; when printing ended, hasCoin = no forgot it, and no flag was left that could give it back.

steps.title: Three flags, eight pictures.
steps.text: Three flags, each yes or no, can show 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations. The machine as built only ever reaches four: waiting (no, no, no), has money (yes, no, no), printing (yes, yes, no) and no paper (no, no, yes). The other four mean nothing, and the code never says what happens in them. Worse, one flag does two jobs. In has money, hasCoin = yes means a coin is in the cup. In printing it still says yes, but that coin went into the box when the print began. So a coin that drops during printing has no flag of its own. Winifrith's line, three lamps can show eight pictures and a good machine only ever shows four, is that count.

steps.title: 17:41, one event at a time.
steps.text: First, at 17:41:20, the first rider's coin set hasCoin = yes. Second, at 17:41:21, their button tipped the cup into the box and set printing = yes. Third, at 17:41:23, the second rider's coin dropped into the cup and set hasCoin = yes, which it already was, so nothing changed. Fourth, at 17:41:24, their button met printing = yes and did nothing. Fifth, at 17:41:25, printed set hasCoin = no, and the program forgot the coin in the cup. After that, the button and cancel both needed hasCoin = yes, so neither could move it, and at 17:42:46 the next rider's ticket tipped it into the box. Riders who waited for the ticket before paying never reached this, which is why the weeks since September ran clean.

steps.title: One object per state.
steps.text: The state pattern, one of the design patterns (s5e06: named shapes of code for problems that keep coming back), makes each state its own object: waiting, has money, printing, no paper. Each object has the same four methods, one per event. The machine keeps one thing: which state object is current. An event is handled in three steps. First, the machine hands the event to the current object's method. Second, that method acts: it tips the cup, opens it, or lights a lamp. Third, it may tell the machine which state comes next. What can go wrong: a method left empty does nothing, just like a flag check that never matches, so every method is written, even as 'can't happen: log it'. In printing, a coin opens the cup into the tray and lights 'wait for the ticket'; the cup was tipped when printing began, so only the new coin comes out.

steps.title: Why not another flag, or a switch?
steps.text: Ignoring coins while printing changes nothing, because the coin still drops into the cup: 23 riders, £46, again. A fourth flag, coinNext, fixes Thursday, but four flags make 16 pictures. On the bench with 14 tickets left, the first 17:41 rider's ticket emptied the roll, and printed set both hasCoin and noPaper to yes, a picture the button was never written for: it tipped the second rider's £2 into the box and printed nothing. A state name with a switch in each event is correct, the same 64 tickets, but each state's rules are split across four switches: a jammed state means four edits, and a missed case is Thursday's bug again. With objects, it is one new class and one changed method.

diagram.aria: The fix, replayed for Thursday at 17:41. The second rider's coin at 17:41:23 is an event. The machine holds the printing object and passes the event to it. The printing object opens the cup into the tray, and the rider has the £2 back. At 17:41:26 the coin goes in again while the state is waiting. After a 4 s print the rider has a ticket at 17:41:31, and the rush ends with 64 tickets for 64 coins.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for Thursday at 17:41. The second rider's coin is still an event, but now the machine passes it to the object for its current state, printing, and printing's coin method has an answer: open the cup into the tray and light 'wait for the ticket'. The rider puts the £2 in again at 17:41:26, when the state is waiting, and has a ticket at 17:41:31. There is no hasCoin left to forget.

fix.title: The fix: one object per state, every event answered
fix.text: Replace the three flags with four state objects, waiting, has money, printing and no paper, each with the same four methods: coin, button, cancel and printed. The machine keeps one current state object and passes every event to it; each method acts and names the next state. Write every method, including 'can't happen: log it'. In printing, a coin opens the cup into the tray and lights 'wait for the ticket'. In printed, the machine goes to no paper when the roll is empty, else to waiting. Add a test that sends every event to every state, so the next state, such as jammed, can't ship with a blank method.

limits: A new event is now the expensive change: a return-ticket button needs a new method in every state class. A shared parent class with a default of 'can't happen: log it' saves typing, but a default can hide a square nobody thought about.

Handing the coin back during printing costs the hurried rider a few seconds: the second 17:41 rider had a ticket 8 s after the first coin, against 5 s for the first rider. A fifth state, printing with the next fare paid, could keep the coin instead, at the price of one more state to write and test.
State objects only make blanks easy to see; someone still has to decide each square. Without a test that sends every event to every state (w03), a method that does nothing can ship just as before.

head: Design
Good
Bad
rows: Short; right whenever riders wait for the ticket.
A coin during printing is forgotten: 23 riders with nothing, £46 with no ticket.
The coin still drops into the cup: the same 23 riders and £46.
16 combinations; with 14 tickets left, one rider's £2 goes in with no paper.
State name, a switch per event
Always one named state: 64 tickets, nobody without.
Each state's rules spread over four switches: a jammed state is four edits.
64 tickets; a coin during printing comes back; a jammed state is one new class.
A new event needs a method in every state class.

explain.seniorTake: When a thing behaves differently depending on its situation, count the situations and name them. Yes-or-no flags look cheap, but n flags make 2 to the power n combinations, most of them meaningless, and the code quietly decides what happens in each one nobody wrote. A state name fixes the counting; state objects also keep each state's rules in one place, so 'what does printing do with a coin?' has exactly one answer, in one method, that a reviewer can find. Pay for it knowingly: new events touch every state. And remember the physical world does not wait for your model. The coin was in the cup whatever the flags said; the design has to give every real thing an owner.

realWorld.title: A Gang of Four pattern
realWorld.text: Wikipedia's article on the state pattern: "The state design pattern is one of twenty-three design patterns documented by the Gang of Four". It lists the first problem the pattern solves as "An object should change its behavior when its internal state changes."

realWorld.title: New states shouldn't disturb old ones
realWorld.text: The same article gives the second problem: state-specific behaviour should be defined independently. "That is, adding new states should not affect the behavior of existing states." Its solution: "A class delegates state-specific behavior to its current state object".

realWorld.title: Without checking the state at every call
realWorld.text: The univ-nantes pattern catalogue, which says "The State pattern is part of the GoF Catalog.", frames the problem as "How to treat an object whose behavior is strongly dependent on its internal state", "without checking this state at each operation call". It gives the pattern's other names as "Objects for States, Envelope-Letter."

realWorld.title: What it buys, and what it may cost
realWorld.text: The same catalogue lists "State-specific behavior is isolated, increasing maintainability." and, against it, "Replacing a conditional by a delegation may reduce performance." On a ticket machine that handles one event a second, the second rarely matters.

realWorld.title: Monstrous conditionals
realWorld.text: Refactoring.guru describes the pattern: "State is a behavioral design pattern that lets an object alter its behavior when its internal state changes." On the switch-and-flags approach it warns: "Most methods will contain monstrous conditionals that pick the proper behavior of a method according to the current state." It adds: "The State pattern is closely related to the concept of a Finite-State Machine".

asked: Design a vending machine or ticket machine.
How would you model its states?
When would you use the state pattern instead of a switch?
interview.answer: I'd start by naming the states rather than reaching for flags: for a coin ticket machine, waiting, has money, printing and out of paper, and the events: coin inserted, ticket button, cancel, print finished, plus a refill. I'd draw the transition table, a row per state and a column per event, and fill every square, including what a coin does while printing, because the physical coin arrives whatever the software thinks. Then the state pattern: an interface with one method per event, one class per state, and a machine that holds its current state object and delegates each event to it; each method acts and returns or sets the next state. Flags are the trap: n yes-or-no flags give 2 to the power n combinations, most of them meaningless, and nothing stops code from reaching one. A single state name with a switch per event is fine for a small, stable machine, but each state's rules then spread across every switch, and a missed case silently does nothing. State objects keep a state's behaviour together, and adding a state is a new class; the trade-off is that adding an event means a new method on every state, often softened with a parent class whose default logs 'can't happen'. Money needs explicit ownership: where each coin is, and who gets it back. I'd test by sending every event to every state.

terms.def: The workshop Winifrith Torvaine left Odgerel, full of half-finished coin machines and automata, each with a paper work order and a program file to match.
A paper slip saying what a client wants made or mended. Each of Winifrith's unfinished machines has one tied to it with string.
The railway in this story: two cars on rails up the cliff from the harbour. A ride costs £2; Aneira is the bottom-station attendant.
A short, steep railway up a cliff, usually with two cars tied together by a cable, so one rises as the other comes down, like the two buckets of a well.
The person on duty where riders board at the harbour. Aneira swaps the cash box, counts it, and keeps a tally of complaints.
Where a coin lands inside the machine. The program either tips it into the cash box when a ticket starts printing, or opens it into the return tray.
The locked box the coins are tipped into. Aneira puts an empty one in at 17:30 and takes it out at 18:30.
The little tray at the front where the machine hands coins back.
The machine's count of tickets printed. Each ticket should match one £2 coin in the box.
A gate where riders tap a bank card and walk through. Sornmouth opened one beside the machine at noon on Thursday, and the coin queue hurried to keep up.
Aneira's paper where she adds a mark for each rider who complains. Thursday's had 23 marks for "it ate my £2".
A note Aneira writes so a rider without a ticket can ride. She wrote one for each of the 23 riders.
A yes-or-no value a program remembers, like a light switch that is on or off. Winifrith's program had three: hasCoin, printing and noPaper.
Winifrith's three flags: a coin is held, a ticket is printing, the roll is empty. During printing, hasCoin still said yes about a coin already in the box.
One way of setting all the flags at once. Three yes-or-no flags give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8; four give 16.
Anything that happens to the machine that the program must react to: a coin drops, a button is pressed, or the printer finishes (printed).
Odgerel's name for the event when the printer finishes a ticket, 4 s after it starts.
Which one of a fixed set of situations a machine is in right now, like a traffic light showing one colour (w03). The ticket machine has four: waiting, has money, printing, no paper.
A state machine written as a grid: a row per state, a column per event, and in each square what happens (w03). A blank square is a question nobody answered.
A bundle of values together with the methods, the actions it can do (s5e04). In the fix, each state is one.
An action an object can do, written as code (s5e04). Each state object has four: coin, button, cancel and printed.
The pattern objects are made from (s5e04). A jammed state means writing one new class.
A list of cases in code, one per possible value, each with its own lines; the program runs the case that matches, like a signpost with one arm per town.
One arm of a switch: the lines that run for one value, such as the state name printing.
A design pattern that makes each state its own object with a method for every event. The machine holds the current state object and passes each event to it.
A named shape of code for a problem that keeps coming back, with the places it fits (s5e06).
Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides, who wrote the 1994 book Design Patterns. The state pattern is one of theirs.
A list of methods a class promises to have, without saying how (s5e04). In the state pattern, every state class has the same interface: coin, button, cancel and printed.
A class others are built from, passing on its methods (s5e04). A parent state class can give every state a default method, such as 'can't happen: log it'.
To hand a job to another object to do. The machine delegates each event to its current state object.
A part of code that runs only if something is true, such as 'if hasCoin and not printing'. Flags and switches are built from them.
A description of a thing as a fixed set of states and the events that move it between them (w03 calls it a state machine). It is always in exactly one state.
How easily code can be changed safely later, by you or someone else.
The fourth flag one commenter suggested: set by a coin during printing and copied into hasCoin when printing ends.
A state the railway asked for later, for when the printer jams. It shows how many places each design must change to add a state.
Short for seconds. A ticket takes 4 s to print.
A small program that runs your code with known inputs and checks the answers. Here: send every event to every state and check each answer.
Winifrith's bench, where Odgerel replays Thursday's rush through a design before it goes into the machine.
One rider, or two close together, stepping up to the machine. 41 groups step up 85 s apart from 17:30:00; 23 are pairs.
The paper the tickets print on: 300 tickets left at 17:30 on Thursday, or 14 on the bench, to see what happens when it runs out mid-rush.

atWork: Look for flags that travel together in your code: isLoading, hasError and isRetrying on a screen; isPaid, isShipped and isCancelled on an order; isConnected and isReconnecting on a phone app. Read-only access to the code is enough. Count them: n flags make 2 to the power n combinations. Write each one down with the situation it stands for, and mark the ones that should be impossible. Then search for code that can reach them, such as a cancel arriving while an order is being shipped, or a retry finishing after the user has left the screen. Many bugs live in exactly those combinations, because each piece of code checks only the flags its author was thinking about. Replace the group with one named state, and where each state behaves very differently, one object per state with a method for every event. Where real money or goods are involved, write down who owns each item in every state, as the coin in the cup here, and add a test that sends every event to every state.

recall.prompt: A self-service car wash bay runs a program with three yes-or-no values: hasToken, washing and waterLow. A token dropped while a wash runs sets hasToken to yes; when the wash ends, the program sets hasToken to no. On Saturday, drivers queued close behind each other, and several lost a token with no wash. What went wrong, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: During a wash hasToken was already yes about the first driver's token, so the second token changed nothing and the end of the wash forgot it
Flags make combinations that nobody named or handled; the machine should be in exactly one named state
One object per state, each answering every event, including a token while washing

recall.model: During a wash, hasToken was already yes, but that yes was about the first driver's token, which had been used. The second token set it to yes again, which changed nothing, and when the wash ended the program set it to no and forgot the token. Three flags make eight combinations, and the code only named some of them; the bay should be in exactly one named state at a time: waiting, paid, washing, out of water. Use the state pattern: one object per state, each with a method for every event, so washing has to answer what a new token does, for example hand it back or hold it for the next wash.

recall.prompt: Winifrith's machine has three yes-or-no flags: hasCoin, printing and noPaper. How many combinations can they show, and how many does the machine as built ever really reach?
recall.why: Each flag doubles the count: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. As built, only waiting (no, no, no), has money (yes, no, no), printing (yes, yes, no) and no paper (no, no, yes) happen. The other four mean nothing, and the code never says what they do.

recall.prompt: Your team's food delivery app keeps an order's status as a name, and five methods (accept, cook, dispatch, deliver, cancel) each switch on that name. The product team wants a new status, on hold. A colleague says: just add a case to each switch. What is the risk, what would you suggest, and what does your suggestion cost?

keyIdeas.idea: One status's rules are spread across every method, so a missed case silently does nothing
Use the state pattern: one class per status with all its behaviour together; a new status is a new class
The cost: a new event or action means a new method in every status class

recall.model: The risk is that the on-hold status's rules end up spread across every method: five switches to edit, and a missed case usually does nothing at all, so an on-hold order might still be dispatched. I'd use the state pattern: one class per status, each with the five methods, and the order holds its current status object and passes each action to it. On hold then becomes one new class with all its behaviour together, and every method has to be written. The cost runs the other way: a new action, such as reschedule, means a new method in every status class, which a parent class with a 'not allowed here' default can soften.

recall.prompt: In the state pattern, what does the ticket machine itself do when a coin drops?
options: It checks each flag in turn, then acts
It passes the coin event to its current state object, which acts and may name the next state
It looks the state name up in a switch with a case for every state
It ignores the coin unless it is waiting
recall.why: The machine keeps only its current state object and passes every event to it. That object's coin method decides what happens: tip, hand back or light a lamp, and which state comes next. Checking flags is the design it replaces; a switch is the other way to name states.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. One object per state, and Aneira's tally stayed empty until January. In early January the railway let the machine take £1 coins too, still £2 a ride. I kept the four states and gave the machine a number, paid: waiting's coin method adds the coin to paid, and moves to has money once paid reaches £2. Since Monday 4 January, Aneira's tally has 9 marks, each for £1. On Sunday 10 January at 15:12 a child put in £1, pressed cancel, and nothing came back.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the child's £1 stay in the machine, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: paid is a hidden flag: waiting now also means 'holding £1', and waiting's cancel, written for an empty cup, gives nothing back
Give part-paid its own state: an object whose cancel opens the cup and whose next £1 moves to has money
Write every method for the new state and test every event in every state

coldCase.model: It's the same mistake in a new place. paid is a hidden flag: the machine says it is waiting, but waiting now also means 'holding £1', so the state has two meanings. Waiting's cancel was written when waiting meant an empty cup, so it says nothing held and hands nothing back, and the child's £1 sat in the cup until the next coin added to it. Give part-paid its own state: an object whose cancel opens the cup into the tray and goes back to waiting, whose next £1 moves to has money, and whose button lights 'insert £1 more'. Then write every method for it, and add the new state to the test that sends every event to every state.
